title: Lone Ranger
caption: An ALMA antenna under airglow, the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A single antenna seems to gaze at a many-colored sky. Green airglow hangs over the horizon, the Large Magellanic Cloud peeks from behind the dish, and the Milky Way sprawls overhead. The antenna is far from alone, though. It belongs to the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, or ALMA, made up of 66 high-precision antennas spread across the Chajnantor plateau high in the Chilean Andes.

The antennas are tuned to millimeter wavelengths, which lie between infrared and radio waves. Human eyes evolved to see visible light, so ALMA's view of the Universe is very different from ours. It picks up light from some of the coldest objects known, including dense star-forming clouds, debris discs around newborn stars and distant galaxies.

ALMA has observed Einstein rings, imaged discs where planets form and found complex organic molecules within such discs. Those findings suggest that our Solar System may not be alone in being able to foster life.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or color details.
understand.eye: The antenna works at millimeter wavelengths that no eye can see, while this photograph records visible light.
